title: Tsunamis
keyIdea: A tsunami is a series of huge waves made when a lot of sea water is pushed all at once, most often by an earthquake under the sea. Landslides and volcanoes can start one too, but wind and tides cannot. In the deep ocean the waves are low, often under 1 m, but as fast as a jet plane. Near land the sea gets shallow, so the waves slow down and grow tall. Strong shaking, the sea rushing far out or a loud roar are warnings: go to high ground at once and stay there, because more waves come.
familyTip: Fill a long baking tray with a little water. Lift one end of a ruler lying flat on the bottom with a quick push and watch the bump race to the far end. Then talk about a family plan: if you are ever at the coast and the ground shakes hard, where is the nearest high ground?

visual.caption: Is it true about tsunamis? Drag each card, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort what starts a tsunami, push the sea floor, find where waves are fastest, spot warning signs and choose what to do.

kid: A tsunami is a set of huge waves. It starts when a lot of sea water is pushed all at once. Most tsunamis start with an earthquake under the sea, when a piece of sea floor jumps up or drops down.
Out in the deep ocean, the waves are low. They may be less than 1 m tall, so ships hardly notice. But they move as fast as a jet plane.
Near the land the sea gets shallow. The waves slow down, but they pile up and grow very tall. They can flood far onto the land.
Nature can warn you. The ground shakes hard, the sea rushes far out, or you hear a roar from the sea. Go to high ground at once. Stay there, because more waves can come for hours.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This supports the National Curriculum in England (geography: describe and understand earthquakes and volcanoes, Key Stage 2) and NGSS 4-ESS3-2 (solutions to reduce the impacts of natural Earth processes on humans). Facts follow NOAA's Tsunami Program, the USGS and the UNESCO IOC Tsunami Glossary: wave speed is about the square root of gravity times depth, so about 700 km/h in 4,000 m of water, about 110 km/h in 100 m and about 35 km/h in 10 m.

The lab has six tasks. Children sort what can and cannot start a tsunami, push a block of sea floor up and watch the water above lift and spread as two waves, tap three places from the fastest wave to the slowest, sort natural warning signs, choose what to do in three moments, and judge three classmates.

Common mistakes. Many children call a tsunami a 'tidal wave' and think tides or wind cause it, picture it as a giant wall of water out at sea, or think it is a single wave, so it is safe after the first one. A dangerous slip is going down to the beach to look when the sea draws back. Stress: go high at once, and stay until officials say it is safe.

practice.hint: What can push all of the sea water at once, from the floor up?
practice.explain: Most tsunamis start with an undersea earthquake that lifts or drops the sea floor. Wind and tides cannot start one.

practice.prompt: A tsunami travels {s} km/h across the deep ocean. How far does it go in {h} hours, in km?
practice.hint: Distance is speed times time. Multiply the speed by the hours.
practice.explain: {s} km/h × {h} hours = {=s*h} km. That is why a tsunami can cross an ocean in less than a day.

choices: In the middle of the sea
practice.hint: In the lab, where did the wave grow when it slowed down?
practice.explain: Near the beach the water is shallow, so the wave slows down and piles up tall. In the deep ocean it is low.

practice.prompt: The first wave arrives at {a} o'clock. Another wave comes {b} hours later. At what o'clock does it arrive?
practice.hint: Add the hours to the time of the first wave.
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} o'clock. Tsunami waves keep coming for hours, so stay on high ground.

practice.prompt: The sea suddenly rushes far out. What should you do?
practice.hint: Is the sea going out a good sign or a warning?
practice.explain: The sea rushing out is a warning that a tsunami may be coming. Go to high ground at once.

pool.prompt: Why is 'tidal wave' the wrong name for a tsunami?
pool.hint: Think about what really starts a tsunami.
pool.explain: Tsunamis come from earthquakes, landslides or volcanoes moving the water, not from tides.

pool.prompt: How tall is a tsunami out in the deep ocean?
choices: It is a wall of water
pool.hint: Do ships out at sea notice it?
pool.explain: In the deep ocean a tsunami is often under 1 m tall, so ships hardly notice. It grows near land.

pool.prompt: Why does a tsunami slow down near the beach?
pool.hint: In the lab, what changed as the wave came close to land?
pool.explain: Tsunami speed depends on the depth of the sea. In shallow water it slows down and grows taller.

pool.prompt: The first tsunami wave has gone back out. What now?
choices: Go and help boats in the harbour
pool.hint: Is a tsunami one wave or many?
pool.explain: A tsunami is a series of waves for hours, and a later one can be the biggest. Stay up high until it is called safe.

pool.prompt: Which of these is a natural warning of a tsunami?
choices: The ground shakes hard near the sea
Small waves on a windy day
pool.explain: Strong shaking near the coast can mean an undersea earthquake. Go to high ground.

pool.prompt: Which can NOT start a tsunami?
choices: A volcano erupting into the sea
pool.hint: Which one only moves the top of the sea?
pool.explain: Wind only makes normal waves on the surface. Landslides and volcanoes can push the whole sea.

pool.hint: The deeper the water, the faster the wave.
pool.explain: In the deep ocean a tsunami goes about 700 km/h, like a jet plane.

pool.prompt: Near the beach a tsunami moves {s} km/h. You can run {r} km/h. How much faster is the wave, in km/h?
pool.hint: Take your running speed away from the wave's speed.
pool.explain: {s} − {r} = {=s-r} km/h faster. You cannot outrun it on the beach, so go to high ground as soon as there is a warning.

pool.prompt: A tsunami crosses the ocean at {s} km/h for {h} hours. How far does it travel, in km?
pool.hint: Multiply the speed by the number of hours.
pool.explain: {s} × {h} = {=s*h} km. Warning centres use this to tell faraway coasts when to expect the waves.
